Security

Security

Trycord enforces who can do what on the server, not in the browser. The server decides, and the interface only shows you what you are allowed to do. This page covers how the pieces are handled, which versions are supported, and the private route for reporting a problem.

Sign-in

Passwords are hashed before they are stored, never kept in a form the server could hand back. Sessions use tokens that can be revoked individually or all at once, and optional two-factor authentication adds a second step for an account that wants it.

Permissions

Community roles and admin powers are checked on the server for every request. The client never decides for itself what you may do; it draws the answer the server gives. A permission that was misspelled in configuration is a startup error rather than a silent grant or refusal.

Uploads

Avatars and file attachments are served through routes that check who is asking, not from a public folder anyone can browse. Upload size is a per-instance setting, and uploads can be switched off entirely.

Moderation and records

Reports, appeals and administrative actions are written to a server-side log, and only people permitted to see them can. An action records who took it and when, and appeals create a record an administrator can act on rather than a message in a private inbox.

Supported versions

Trycord is developed continuously on main. Security fixes land on the current codebase and are included in later releases. There is no long-term-support branch.

ComponentSupported
Server (main)Yes
Web client (main)Yes
Latest desktop releaseYes
Older desktop releasesNo
Unmaintained forks or modified buildsNo

If you self-host Trycord, keep your server updated with the latest supported code and apply fixes promptly. The changelog is where releases are described.

Reporting a vulnerability

Report privately, and only when it could allow unauthorized access, data exposure, privilege escalation, or other harm to users or self-hosted instances.

Preferred route: use GitHub's private vulnerability reporting. Do not open a public issue for a security vulnerability.

A useful report says what you found, where, how to reproduce it, and what the impact could be. If you can, include the version or commit, the configuration that matters, and a minimal reproduction. Please do not test against instances that have not agreed to it, and do not access, change, or keep other people's data while demonstrating an issue.

OPERATOR: a security contact for this instance, if you want one besides the project

If you run an instance

Your users' security is your responsibility, because the data is yours. Keep the server updated, set a unique JWT_SECRET, put the service behind TLS, and review the settings that widen access before you turn them on. The documentation covers the options that have security consequences.

Operator note. Every instance serves this page, so it stays generic. Edit it in Admin, or edit the file public/security.html, to add your own security contact or disclosure policy where the placeholder appears.
